messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] multiple qtl model for binary trait, with potential for sex-linkage?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] multiple qtl model for binary trait, with potential for sex-linkage?
messages.body_plain:
Since you're doing a backcross with only males, the X chromosome will behave like the autosomes, with two possible genotypes at any position, and so in this case you need not worry about special treatment for the X; multiple QTL analysis will work fine as implemented.

karl

On Aug 30, 2012, at 12:12 PM, HASmith wrote:

> Hi. I'm new to QTL analysis, but looking to set up an analysis for a binary trait, backcross, and need to preserve the distinction of the X chromosome v autosomes as there's the potential for involvement of a sex-linked locus affecting the trait. We have a single covariate (best coded as binary). Only males were sequenced, so perhaps due to having just the one X chromosome ( it's a traditional XY system) that simplifies matters a little.
>
> My concern is that it seems a multiple QTL model is the most rigorous approach, from reading Broman's book, but the new manual makes me fear that the multiple QTL model doesn't work for sex chromosomes (text below). Is this correct? I'd like to use R/QTL but am wondering if I need to go to another application (randomForests?).
>
> Thank you,
> Hilary
>

messages.subject: Re: Toward a more efficient analysis of QTL x covariate interactions
messages.subject_clean: Toward a more efficient analysis of QTL x covariate interactions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

Sorry to be a bother again.  I have now completed running the
interactive model for all of my transcription phenotypes.  I could run
about 2500 in a batch given the memory constraints in R, but this was
still way faster than running the phenotypes one at a time in a loop.

I then went back to spot check to make sure that the results I
obtained through the batch runs matched with running the traits
individually.  I set the same seed for the individual phenotype runs
as for the batch runs. However, for some reason I got different p-
values for the same QTLs in the batch and individual phenotype runs.
Is it possible that the permutations are different in the batch runs
and the individual phenotype runs, even if the seed is the same?

Thanks again,

David

On Aug 28, 2:07 pm, David Lowry <davidbryantlo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Excellent!
>
> Thanks again Karl.
>
> David
>
> On Aug 27, 6:32 pm, Karl Broman <kbro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
> > The phenotypes will be permuted in parallel.  There should be no problem doing it this way; in fact it is preferred (to maintain the correlations among phenotypes) should you want to make some correction for the search across phenotypes as well as the search across the genome.
>
> > karl
>
> > On Aug 27, 2012, at 1:36 PM, David Lowry <davidbryantlo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > > Thanks Karl!
>
> > > I have been spending some more time on the problem and it appears that
> > > I can accomplish the analysis using the pheno.col=1:25662 statement
> > > (see code below).  This is incredibly faster than running the
> > > permutations one at a time in a loop.  My concern is whether all the
> > > phenotypes will start with the same seed.  I know that starting with
> > > the same seed is very important for comparing the two models and so I
> > > wanted to check with you that what I am doing is correct.  From quick
> > > glances at the output for a few phenotypes, it appears that the
> > > permutations all do start with the same seed.  Here is the code:
>
> > > out.a=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
> > > method=c("hk"))
> > > out.u=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
> > > model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"))
> > > set.seed(54955149)
> > > operm.a <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x,
> > > model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=6)
> > > set.seed(54955149)
> > > operm.u <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=1:25662, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
> > > model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=6)
> > > out.u <- c(out.u, out.u-out.a, labels=c("f","i"))
> > > operm.u <- cbind(operm.u, operm.u - operm.a, labels=c("f","i"))
> > > tabbycol_25662<-summary(out.u, perms=operm.u, format="tabByCol",
> > > pvalues=TRUE, ci.function="lodint")
>
> > > write.table(tabbycol_25662, file = "Tab_by_dry_SNP_cyto_25662.txt",
> > > quote=FALSE, row.name <http://row.name>=FALSE)
>
> > > Thanks again,
>
> > > David
>
> > > On Aug 27, 8:26 am, Karl Broman <kbro...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >> I expect it's the permutations that are taking all the time?
> > >> I would first do the actual analysis and study it.
>
> > >> You have to expect the permutation tests to take a long time.
> > >> You'll need more processors.
>
> > >> karl
>
> > >> On Aug 24, 2012, at 7:02 AM, David Lowry wrote:
>
> > >>> Dear Karl,
>
> > >>> I am currently trying to conduct an eQTL analysis in Arabidopsis and
> > >>> want to evaluate cytoplasm x eQTL interactions.  Following the
> > >>> examples in section 7.2 of the rQTL book on QTL x covariate
> > >>> interactions I wrote the following loop:
>
> > >>> k<-1
>
> > >>> while(k<=25000){
> > >>> out.a=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
> > >>> method=c("hk"))
> > >>> out.u=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
> > >>> model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"))
> > >>> set.seed(54955149)
> > >>> operm.a <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
> > >>> method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=32)
> > >>> set.seed(54955149)
> > >>> operm.u <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
> > >>> model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=32)
> > >>> out.u <- c(out.u, out.u-out.a, labels=c("f","i"))
> > >>> operm.u <- cbind(operm.u, operm.u - operm.a, labels=c("f","i"))
> > >>> a<-summary(out.u, perms=operm.u, pvalues=TRUE)
> > >>> all<-cbind(all, a)
> > >>> write.table(all, file = "eQTL_Cyto_normal_perm_25000_dry.txt",
> > >>> quote=FALSE, row.name <http://row.name>=FALSE)
> > >>> k<-k+1}
>
> > >>> Unfortunately, even with the 32 processors this analysis runs very
> > >>> slowly.  I was only able to complete about 350 phenotypes in 24
> > >>> hours.  I usually can complete about 5000 phenotypes in 24 hours with
> > >>> one processor using the pheno.col=1:5000 option.  Since my analysis
> > >>> involves so many phenotypes (~75000), I am trying to figure out a way
> > >>> that I can make the analysis more efficient, without creating many
> > >>> scripts.  Do you have any suggestions?  In the end, I need to estimate
> > >>> p-values in order to implement a False Discovery Rate.
>
> > >>> Thank you very much,
>
> > >>> David
>

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] A simple bug in mqmscanall?
messages.body_plain:
Ideally we will revise the MQM-related functions to have a pheno.col argument for selecting phenotype columns.

karl

On Sep 11, 2012, at 2:16 PM, John wrote:

> Hi,
>
> As you know, read.cross treats "id" as a phenotype, but scanone would ignore it it during analysis.
>
> However, it appears to me that the mqmscanall in my copy qtl (1.25) does not ignore "id" and go on performing genome scan as if id was a normal phenotype.
>
> mqmheatmap didn't seem to recognize this either, so when I feed the mqmmulti object such produced, mqmheatmap would give a "phenotype id is not numeric" error.
>
> A workaround is available for that (ripping off the id from the original cross), I think this still needs to be fixed...
>
> In the long term, I think, the "id" should actually be separated from cross$pheno so that coders would not confuse the real nature of "id".
>
> Cheers,
>
> John Ma

messages.subject_clean: Question on error message with scantwo
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am analyzing a binary trait with rqtl, and while scanone works, I obtain an error message with scantwo that I do not understand. I would greatly appreciate any insight on why this is occurring and how to fix it. (By the way -- I am using the script from https://github.com/dstern/read_cross_msg to create the cross object, which does give a map in base pairs -- so I was told to ignore the warning about the long chromosomes at the end of this by the author of the script. I just output a summary of the cross object in case this is helpful to understand my question).
Thank you for any insight.
Best,
Hilary

> S1_P4_em = scanone(P4, chr=c("2L", "2R", "3L", "3R", "X"), model="binary", method="em", pheno.col=binphe)
> S2_P4_em_autosomes = scantwo(P4, chr=c("2L", "2R", "3L", "3R"), model="binary", method="em", pheno.col=binphe)

messages.body_plain:
Try running scantwo with argument assumeCondIndep=TRUE

scantwo uses the joint genotype probabilities at two positions,
given the marker data. I suspect that these calculations are
incompatible with the results of David Stern's code, and it may
be that the above will work.

If it doesn't work, I'll need to look on the intermediate results from
Stern's code to figure out how to get it to work.

karl

messages.subject: p-values (through permutations) for FDR calculation using q-values
messages.subject_clean: p-values (through permutations) for FDR calculation using q-values
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

I’m conducting an QTL study in a mouse intercross.  A challenge is figuring out how to control for multiple testing with many phenotypes (we have n=1841).  One method is using q-values/FDRs based on permutations: to use the package q-value (Storey et al, 2003) I require a list of p-values (instead of LOD-scores) for my R/qtl scanone results for each phenotype.

Is there any way to get a p-value for each marker (as I get for the LOD-scores), instead of the summary function (which I used below), where I just get the highest LOD-score for each chromosome?

for(k in 1:(length(cross0$pheno))) {
out.1=  scanone(cross0, pheno.col=2, method="em", model="normal")
operm.f2<- scanone(cross0, pheno.col=2, method="em", model="normal" , n.perm=1000)
a <- summary (out.1, perms=operm.f2, format="tabByCol", pvalues=TRUE)
write.csv(a,file = paste("C:/Documents and Settings/rQTL_outputFiles_pvalues/pvalues_",names(cross0$pheno[k]),".txt",sep=""))
}

Thanks so much for your help,

Annette

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] p-values for FDR using permutations (output for q-Package)
messages.body_plain:
With just one phenotype and no X-chromosome-specific permutations, you could just do something like this:

  data(fake.bc)
  fake.bc <- calc.genoprob(fake.bc)
  out <- scanone(fake.bc, method="hk")
  operm <- scanone(fake.bc, method="hk", n.perm=1000)
  pval <- sapply(out[,3], function(a,b) mean(b >= a), opera)

In place of sapply in that last line, you could use a for loop:

  pval <- rep(NA, nrow(out))
  for(i in 1:nrow(out))
     pval[i] <- mean(operm >= out[i,3])

But these are p-values adjusting for the genome scan (and so controlling the family-wise error rate, FWER).

It's not clear to me exactly what sort of p-values you want, for your FDR calculations.

I'd recommend against using FDR control for the scan across genome, but I can see using it to handle the multiple phenotypes, if you have *many* phenotypes (like 20,000).  But in that case I'd focus on a single p-value per phenotype.

karl
